newsitem.title: JAPAN: Railway land sale signals revival in Japan market.
newsitem.headline: Railway land sale signals revival in Japan market.

text.p: Japan's sluggish real estate market is expected to show some signs of revival after Monday's sale of three prime tracts in central Tokyo, analysts said.
"The good news is there is some activity, that there are people out there looking for real estate," said Steven Weiler, an analyst at Jardine Fleming Securities.

JNR Settlement Corp said idle land located near Ginza, Tokyo's premier shopping district and once a freight station owned by the defunct Japanese National Railways, sold for 372.3 billion yen ($3.05 billion). The sum exceeded most analysts' expectations of up to 300 billion yen ($2.45 billion).

Weiler said the land's price was "reasonable" and that it was sold at about market value -- around 80 percent lower than sky-high peaks reached during the "bubble economy" in the late 1980s. At that time, he estimated, the land would have been worth just under two trillion yen ($16.3 billion).

JNR said successful bidders for the three lots were a group led by Dentsu Inc, a group led by Mitsui Fudosan Co Ltd, including Matsushita Electric Works and Alderney Investment Pte Ltd, and a group led by Nippon Television Network Corp.

"That one of Japan's largest developers, Mitsui Fudosan, hasn't embarked on new commercial development over the last few years but has decided to do so now shows a sense of bottoming out in prices for some types of land," said Junichi Shiomoto, an analyst at Nomura Research Institute.
Analysts also pointed to the participation of Alderney Investments Pte, a joint venture of Hong Kong and Singaporean business interests, as a sign of improving sentiment.
"An Asian global player has come into the market and bought -- they think the Tokyo market is cheap when compared with other Asian markets," said Shiomoto.
Real estate values have been sliding since the bubble burst in the early 1990s.
But analysts also cautioned that only "blue-chip" sections of the land market were likely to benefit.
"Good property, blue chip investments will do well but bad property is still going to remain bad property," said Yoshinobu Yamada, an analyst at Merrill Lynch.

The sale's success also sounded a long-missed positive note for Japan's ailing banking sector -- the centre of a stock sell-off over the last two weeks. Most Japanese banks are struggling with mountainous bad loans, many of which were made to the real estate sector and used property as collateral.
Analysts said that while the sale was hardly a cure-all, there was some light at the end of the tunnel.
"Banks know now that if they have a tidy piece of property, one with a good location, then it can sell," said Shiomoto. ($1=122 yen)
